title: ⭐⭐ Practice: how much, how many at once, and what the figures allow

questions.prompt: Hedi's class went up the hill above Gafsa to plant trees. They took the school van, and the van reached the top without any trouble. Complete the note Hedi wrote that evening: "The track up the hill was ___ for the van to pass."

options.text: wide enough
narrow enough
too narrow
enough wide

questions.explanation: "wide enough" is the answer: adjective + enough + to says that the action took place, and the van did reach the top. It is also the quality the van needed, since a van passes when there is width, not when there is a lack of it. "narrow enough" is correctly built but chooses the wrong adjective: it would mean the track was narrow to a sufficient degree, which is what you say of a path meant for a bicycle, not of a track a van has to get up. "too narrow" reports the opposite of what happened: too + adjective + to always means the action did NOT take place, so the van would have turned back. And "enough wide" puts the word in the wrong place: of the four adverbs of degree, enough is the only one that follows the adjective instead of standing before it.

questions.prompt: A school magazine has sent this line to the printer: "The last two birds of the species died in the island reserve in 1962, and the species is now endangered." The sub-editor stops the page, because one word makes the sentence untrue. Which correction does she make?

options.text: Replace "species" with "wildlife".
Replace "endangered" with "in danger".
Replace "died" with "drowned".
Replace "endangered" with "extinct".

questions.explanation: "Replace \"endangered\" with \"extinct\"." is the correction. The line says the last two birds died, so no living member is left anywhere, and that is exactly what extinct means. Endangered means at risk of disappearing, which supposes there are still animals alive to save. "Replace \"endangered\" with \"in danger\"." changes the words without changing the meaning, so the sentence stays just as untrue. "Replace \"species\" with \"wildlife\"." swaps a countable word for a collective one: wildlife names the wild animals and birds of a place taken together, and cannot name one single kind of bird. And "Replace \"died\" with \"drowned\"." invents a cause of death the line never gives, and leaves the false word untouched.

questions.prompt: Nizar is closing his talk on the new dam. He has two facts, and he does not want his audience to hear the second one as a small extra: the dam holds the winter water, and it supplies the town with electricity. Which closing line puts the two facts on the same level?

options.text: The dam holds the winter water, and it supplies the town with electricity.
The dam not only holds the winter water but also supplies the town with electricity.
The dam holds the winter water; it supplies the town with electricity too.
The dam holds not only the winter water but also supplies the town with electricity.

questions.explanation: "The dam not only holds the winter water but also supplies the town with electricity." is the line: not only and but also form a pair whose whole function is addition, and whose effect is to announce the second member as counting at least as much as the first. Both members here are verb phrases, holds the winter water and supplies the town with electricity, so the two sides are of the same grammatical kind. "The dam holds the winter water, and it supplies the town with electricity." is correct English, but plain and is neutral: it lines the two facts up without telling the audience that the second one matters, which is precisely what Nizar asked for. "The dam holds the winter water; it supplies the town with electricity too." is correct as well, and does even less: too at the end of a sentence marks an addition as an afterthought. And "The dam holds not only the winter water but also supplies the town with electricity." is broken: not only has been placed after the verb, so the first member is a noun phrase and the second a verb phrase, and the law of the structure is that the two members must be of the same kind.

questions.prompt: A club in Nabeul has printed this poster. "OUR WATER WEEK. Litres used per person per day in the four classes that took part: class 1, 96 litres; class 2, 118 litres; class 3, 121 litres; class 4, 89 litres. National average: 120 litres." The club now wants a headline under the figures. Which of these four claims do its own figures NOT support?

options.text: Class 4 used the least water of the four.
Only one class went above the national average.
Class 3 used more than twice as much water as class 4.
Three of the four classes stayed below the national average.

questions.explanation: "Class 3 used more than twice as much water as class 4." is the claim the poster cannot make: class 3 used 121 litres and class 4 used 89, and twice 89 is 178, so class 3 used about a third more, not more than double. The gap is real, but the word twice doubles it a second time. "Class 4 used the least water of the four." is supported: 89 is the lowest of the four figures. "Only one class went above the national average." is supported too: 121 is the single figure above 120. And "Three of the four classes stayed below the national average." is supported by the same reading: 96, 118 and 89 are all under 120. A poster is judged on the figures printed beside it, and one sentence that goes further than they do costs it the other three.

questions.prompt: Two pupils describe the same dry river bed for the school magazine. Wassim writes: "By August the river bed was as white as a page." Mouna writes: "By August the river bed was a white page." Which statement about the two sentences is true?

options.text: Wassim wrote a simile, Mouna wrote a metaphor.
Wassim wrote a metaphor, Mouna wrote a simile.
Both wrote similes, because both compare the river bed to a page.
Both wrote metaphors, because neither of them uses the word like.

questions.explanation: "Wassim wrote a simile, Mouna wrote a metaphor." is true. A simile announces its comparison with a sign, like or as ... as, and Wassim uses as ... as. A metaphor makes the same comparison with no sign at all: Mouna does not say the river bed was like a page, she says it WAS one. "Wassim wrote a metaphor, Mouna wrote a simile." reverses the two, and gives the name metaphor to the sentence that carries the sign. "Both wrote similes, because both compare the river bed to a page." mistakes the definition: the two figures both compare, and what separates them is not the comparison but whether it is announced. And "Both wrote metaphors, because neither of them uses the word like." forgets that like is not the only sign of a simile: as ... as is the other, and Wassim uses it.

questions.prompt: A teacher writes this sentence on the board: "The leaflet was too technical for the pupils to follow." She then asks the class which two plain facts she started from before she joined them into that one sentence. Which pair is it?

options.text: The leaflet was technical. The pupils followed it with difficulty.
The leaflet was not technical enough. The pupils did not follow it.
The leaflet was technical. The pupils had to follow it anyway.
The leaflet was very technical. The pupils did not follow it.

questions.explanation: "The leaflet was very technical. The pupils did not follow it." is the pair. Your grammar summary takes its own example apart in exactly this way: You are too young to understand, in brackets, you do not understand because you are too young. So too + adjective gives the first fact and the infinitive gives the second one, in the negative. "The leaflet was technical. The pupils followed it with difficulty." keeps the difficulty but lets the reading happen, which is what the structure rules out. "The leaflet was not technical enough. The pupils did not follow it." reverses the first fact: not technical enough would mean the leaflet was too simple, and only the opposite adjective turns a too sentence into a not enough one, as in too thin and not thick enough. And "The leaflet was technical. The pupils had to follow it anyway." adds an obligation that appears nowhere in the sentence.
